clue.text: Sophisticated guy - don't give him a hot dog!

blocks.note: the plain sense: a suave, stylish man

blocks.clueFragment: don't give him a hot dog!
blocks.note: the setter's reading: a feline that is not hot, so the opposite of a hot canine

explanation.surface: Advice on catering for a suave man: he won't want street food.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke flips both halves of 'hot dog': not hot but chilled, not a canine but a feline.
explanation.definitionFit: Jazz slang for a stylish, relaxed and fashionable man is exactly this phrase.

clue.text: Time of arrival sees John hot on Robin

blocks.note: Sir John Birt, Director-General of the BBC in the 1990s
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
Sir Robin Day, the British television political interviewer

explanation.surface: A broadcasting scene: one BBC man piling in on another just as somebody arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names are British broadcasters: John Birt ran the BBC and Robin Day was its famously combative interviewer. 'Robin' looks like the bird but is the surname-giver.
explanation.definitionFit: The anniversary of the day you were born marks your arrival into the world, so it is your time of arrival.

clue.text: Sick? On the contrary: it's somebody's 2 in song

blocks.note: the reply that contradicts the question just asked
the opposite of sick is well

explanation.surface: A patient asked if they are ill answers that, quite the reverse, they are fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer to 'Sick?' is 'No, well'. 2 refers to 2-down, BIRTHDAY: the carol 'The First Nowell' celebrates the birth of Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: Nowell is the carol word for Christmas, which celebrates the birth of Christ, as in 'The First Nowell'.

clue.text: With the 2nd 2 one sees people entering another gulf

definitions.note: a thematic definition: Tuesday's child, born on the second day of the week, is full of grace

indicators.note: another version of the word gulf is its letters made into something different
to enter is to go inside, so the people go into the middle of the other word

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a race is a people or nation

explanation.surface: A traveller on the second birthday sees people moving into a second gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme is the rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face, Tuesday's child is full of grace...'; 2 is 2-down, BIRTHDAY, and the 2nd birth day is Tuesday.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuesday's child is full of grace in the nursery rhyme, and being full of grace is being elegant and poised.

clue.text: With the 3rd 2 one would nearly enter successive notes

definitions.note: a thematic definition: Wednesday's child is full of woe

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the final letter of the word would is dropped
to enter is to go inside, so the notes go into the shortened word

blocks.note: taken as written before losing its last letter
E and F are neighbouring notes of the scale

explanation.surface: Someone on their third birthday nearly walks into a run of musical notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'would' does double duty: it ends the thematic definition and is also the word that loses its D. The 3rd birth day is Wednesday, whose child is 'full of woe'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wednesday's child is full of woe in the rhyme, and being full of woe is being miserable and sad.

clue.text: Heat preserver from nethermost hell

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the following word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: the letters run inside this word, between NE and T
surface padding: completes the picture of the lowest depths

explanation.surface: Something that keeps heat in, coming from the lowest depths of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hell' finishes the surface's joke about heat and is not part of the wordplay; the letters sit within 'nethermost'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vacuum flask keeps hot drinks hot by insulating them, so it preserves heat.

clue.text: Voices of disapproval about fool getting mackerel

definitions.note: mackerel serves as a plural here, matching the plural answer

indicators.note: about means around, so the jeers wrap around the fool

blocks.note: jeers from a crowd
a nit is a silly person, short for nitwit

explanation.surface: A crowd jeers at an idiot who has landed a catch of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: A nit is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonitos are fish of the mackerel and tuna family, so they are a kind of mackerel.

clue.text: Light roll gives spirit to revolutionary

blocks.note: brio is vigour, liveliness
Che Guevara, the archetypal revolutionary

explanation.surface: A snack bun gives a guerrilla fighter energy.
explanation.definitionFit: A brioche is a soft, buttery French bread bun, so it is a light kind of bread roll.

clue.text: With the 5th 2 one is to attend between Frank and Edward

definitions.note: a thematic definition: Friday's child is loving and giving

blocks.note: frank and open both mean candid
to attend to a sound is to hear it
Ted is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Someone on their fifth birthday is told to go between two men, Frank and Edward.
explanation.walkthrough: The 5th birth day is Friday, and 'Friday's child is loving and giving'. Between Frank and Edward simply places the middle piece between the other two.
explanation.definitionFit: Loving and giving describes a generous, warm nature, which is what kindly and generous in spirit means.

clue.text: Liberal revolution gets the spirit

definitions.note: defined through the phrase Blithe Spirit, Shelley's skylark and Noel Coward's play

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters of the abbreviation are churned

blocks.note: LIB is the short form of Liberal
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political party's uprising finds its soul.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the word that goes before 'spirit' in Shelley's 'Hail to thee, blithe spirit!' and Coward's play. It also completes the theme: Sunday's child is 'bonny and blithe'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the classic companion of spirit, from Shelley's skylark ode and Coward's comedy, meaning carefree and cheerful.

clue.text: In the cinema Mary's choice falls on Harrison

blocks.note: your pick is your choice
Harrison Ford, the film actor

explanation.surface: At the pictures, Mary decides she fancies Harrison Ford.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Pickford was a silent film star and a founder of United Artists, the screen's best-known Mary.

clue.text: With the 6th 2 one is a witch - about right, a feminist!

definitions.note: a thematic definition: Saturday's child works hard for its living

indicators.note: about means around, so the witch is wrapped around what follows

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
Andrea Dworkin, the American radical feminist writer
a hag is an ugly old witch

explanation.surface: An outburst calling a feminist a witch, on the sixth birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: The 6th birth day is Saturday, and 'Saturday's child works hard for its living'. The feminist's surname is the long middle chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Working hard for a living is diligent, industrious labour, which this compound adjective describes.

clue.text: Tall chap lying down found life real and earnest

blocks.note: long and tall both describe great length
a fellow is a man, a chap

explanation.surface: A tall man resting finds life serious business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying down' tells us the pieces sit side by side in an across entry. The definition quotes 'A Psalm of Life': 'Life is real! Life is earnest!'
explanation.definitionFit: The American poet wrote 'Life is real! Life is earnest!' in A Psalm of Life, so he is who found it so.

clue.text: Plagal mode: get windy after taking syringe: I only hope AA can make it

linkWords: I only hope AA can make it

blocks.note: hypo is short for hypodermic syringe
from Aeolus, god of the winds

explanation.surface: A fraught breakdown: windy after an injection, hoping the motoring rescue service turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail is a joke: the AA is Britain's motoring breakdown service, and the answer needs its two As among the cluster of vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: In church music each authentic mode has a plagal partner prefixed hypo-, and this is the plagal form of the Aeolian mode.

clue.text: PTO for the complete attendant

blocks.note: something over is finished, complete
a page is a young attendant

explanation.surface: An instruction to turn over, addressed to the perfect servant.
explanation.definitionFit: PTO stands for 'please turn over', telling the reader the text continues on the next leaf.

clue.text: Shearer keeping Halliwell from Constantine, perhaps

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the footballer holds the singer

blocks.note: Alan Shearer, the England football captain
Geri Halliwell, Ginger of the Spice Girls

explanation.surface: A footballer protecting a pop star from a man called Constantine.
explanation.walkthrough: Shearer looks like a sheep-shearer, but it is the footballer; Constantine is a city, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Constantine is a large city in north-eastern Algeria, so someone from there is an example of a native of that country.

clue.text: Refuse is always increasing

blocks.note: with the 'is' before it: something that is increasing gains
ay (or aye) is an old word for ever

explanation.surface: Rubbish keeps piling up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a noun meaning rubbish, but it is the verb to deny.
explanation.definitionFit: To deny or contradict a claim is to oppose it, close to declining or rejecting it.

clue.text: See 12
Conductor's role reversing old car

indicators.note: reversing means going backwards, so the word for role is read from its end

blocks.note: Sir Simon Rattle, the British conductor
a part is a role in a play

explanation.surface: A conductor's job involves driving an old banger backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Conductor could be a bus or train conductor or an electrical one; here it is Simon Rattle.
explanation.definitionFit: A rickety, noisy old vehicle is called this, from the rattling it makes on the road.

clue.text: Was attracted by authority in its entirety?

indicators.note: in places the approval inside the Latin phrase for wholly

blocks.note: from the Latin 'in toto', in its entirety
giving the OK means giving authority to proceed

explanation.surface: Someone drawn to authority wholesale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' works twice: as the insertion signal and as the first word of the Latin phrase 'in toto', meaning wholly.
explanation.definitionFit: If you took to someone or something, you came to like it, so you were drawn to it.

clue.text: With the 1st 2 one is quite often with 22

definitions.note: a thematic definition: Monday's child is fair of face
22 is GOOD; quite good can be said as this word plus good

blocks.note: first meaning: born on Monday, the first birth day, and so fair of face
second meaning: an adverb for quite, often paired with the answer to 22

explanation.walkthrough: The 1st birth day is Monday, and 'Monday's child is fair of face'. 22-across is GOOD, giving the phrase PRETTY GOOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair of face means good-looking, and as an adverb the same word means fairly, as in 'pretty good'.

clue.text: With the last 2 one is a piece of, say, 7 and 10, this and 17's outside

definitions.text: With the last 2 one is a piece of, say, 7 and 10, this and 17's outside

blocks.note: the setter's reading: born on Sunday, the last birth day, the child is 'bonny and blithe

blocks.clueFragment: a piece of, say, 7 and 10, this and 17's outside
blocks.note: the rhyme's last line: 10 is the blithe entry, 17's outside letters give a word for merry, and the answer is 'this'

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme ends 'But the child that is born on the Sabbath day is bonny and blithe, and good and gay'. GAY is GAINSAY without its INSA; 7 stands loosely for 'bonny'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday's child is said in the rhyme to be virtuous and well-behaved, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: A stroke by the French: provide a detachment

blocks.note: un is French for a
coup is French for a stroke or blow
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A French master stroke supplies a military unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the French' signals all three pieces are French words, though only the last is literally 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Unhitching railway wagons separates them, so it brings about a detachment of one from another.

clue.text: "You stinker!" cried Archimedes

blocks.note: someone who reeks is a stinker

explanation.surface: Archimedes, leaping from his bath, insults someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Archimedes leapt naked from his bath shouting this word, so a smell joke is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes is said to have shouted the Greek for 'I have found it' when he discovered the principle of displacement.

clue.text: With the 4th 2 one has service backing for African country

definitions.note: a thematic definition: Thursday's child has far to go

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the service is read in reverse

blocks.note: the Royal Air Force, one of the armed services
Togo in West Africa

explanation.surface: On a fourth birthday, an air force supports an African state.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4th birth day is Thursday, and 'Thursday's child has far to go'; the definition is the rhyme's line itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Thursday's child in the nursery rhyme has a long journey ahead, the phrase quoted directly.

clue.text: One who won't drink isn't commonly going to convict

blocks.note: a means one
TT is teetotal, abstaining from alcohol
ain't is the colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A teetotaller in dialect speech insists he is not about to lock anyone up.
explanation.definitionFit: To attaint is an old legal verb meaning to condemn someone, especially for treason.
